rationale:
Evidence: all eight designs went off track in all 60 trials. max_error sits at 0.061 to 0.066 m against the 0.06 m limit whatever the gain (kp 1.2 to 3), speed (0.6 to 1.6), sensor span (+/-0.03 to +/-0.06 m) or mass. Progress is nearly fixed by track (oval about 0.12 to 0.17, s-bend about 0.04 to 0.07), so the robot leaves the line at roughly the same early point each time. The parameter sweeps have stopped moving the outcome. The untested factors are drivetrain geometry (wheel_track has only been 0.12 to 0.14, wheel_radius only 0.03) and sensor y position (all sensors have been 0.04 m or further ahead of the axle, so steering lag is large).

Changes: (1) Sensors moved to y = 0.02, close to the axle, to cut the steering lag that a sensor 6 cm ahead introduces. (2) Geometry otherwise kept from iteration 8: seven sensors at x = -0.03 to +0.03, 12 mm footprints. (3) wheel_track widened to 0.18 (top of range), which lowers the yaw rate per unit wheel-speed difference and should reduce overshoot. (4) wheel_radius raised to 0.05 (top of range), which gives more ground speed per PWM count and so a faster run at the same base_speed. (5) base_speed raised from 0.6 to 0.8 to test whether the wider drivetrain can hold the line at more speed. (6) kp raised from 1.2 to 2.0, since the lower yaw rate from the wider track reduces the effective gain, and the weights are small. kd raised to 1.0 to damp the faster response. ki 0.3 kept for the motor-mismatch bias. line_loss stays last_direction.

This is a diagnostic as much as an improvement attempt. Expected result: max_error below about 0.05 m and fewer line-loss events. Completion remains unlikely. If max_error still reaches 0.06, the controller structure (e.g. signal scaling or line-loss handling) is the next suspect, not the gains.
